title: Learned certificates: train a model to output C given p, verify by exact arithmetic (AlphaProof-style)
connection: The solution search is 'find C'; a learned prior on C (given features of p) could shrink the search and, more importantly, expose which C-values are 'predictable'.
why: A predictable C-function would be an identity candidate; non-predictability calibrates against covering-type proofs.
first_step: Train a regressor from p-features to log C_min(p); compare against baseline (median); inspect residuals vs p mod 840.

title: Mine the Lean 'Erdős problems' formalisation project for ES-adjacent lemmas
connection: Erdős problems site + Lean formalisation efforts (e.g. Erdős #306 nearly formalised). ES is Erdős problem #… (check the erdosproblems.com number) — see what lemma infrastructure exists for unit-fraction problems there.
why: Infrastructure reuse; cheap.
first_step: Visit https://www.erdosproblems.com and search 'Straus'; check the associated GitHub for Lean files.

title: Streaming/sketching: minimal information about p needed to construct a solution
connection: Communication-complexity framing: Alice knows p mod M, Bob knows ⌊p/M⌋; how much communication is needed to agree on an ES solution? If O(1) bits suffice for some M, that's a covering system; if Θ(log p), solutions are 'global'.
why: A clean quantitative version of 'ES is not local' (Mordell–Schinzel says polynomial-local fails; this asks for any protocol).
first_step: Empirically: for M = 840, compute for each residue class r the size of the smallest 'dictionary' of solution templates (c,d) needed to cover all primes ≡ r up to 10⁶; growth with the range.

title: Property testing: can one certify ES(p) with o(log p) queries to an oracle for the factorisation of 4Cp+1?
connection: Query complexity of the existence problem given a factorisation oracle: how many C must be queried in the worst case (empirically) before a winner is found? The query sequence design (adaptive vs non-adaptive) is the algorithmic skeleton of a proof.
why: Worst-case query counts over p ≤ 10⁸ calibrate the 'depth' of a proof (K queries ⇒ a K-case argument).
first_step: Record C_min(p) distribution (non-adaptive) and design an adaptive rule (choose next C based on factorisation of previous 4Cp+1); measure the max number of queries for p ≤ 10⁷.

title: Compressed sensing / sparse recovery: f(p) as a sparse combination of character sums
connection: Express f(p) (or its Type I part) as Σ_χ c_χ χ(p) over characters of various moduli (it's not periodic, but truncated versions are); sparse recovery finds the dominant characters. Dominant terms = the identities that matter most.
why: Quantifies 'how periodic is f(p)' beyond Mordell's mod 840; a sparse spectrum would suggest a near-covering.
first_step: Fit f(p) − A log²p on p ≤ 10⁷ against characters mod M ≤ 10⁴ with LASSO; list top characters.

title: Grover-style amplitude amplification is irrelevant, but the quantum query lower bound technique (adversary method) applies to classical 'how many C must be tried'
connection: Adversary bounds give lower bounds on queries needed to find a winning C against a worst-case p; translated classically: any proof that tries C in a fixed order needs ≥ max C_min(p) cases.
why: Makes precise that a 'list of templates' proof must have unbounded length — reinforcing Mordell–Schinzel from an algorithmic angle, but also showing adaptive proofs are not bound by it.
first_step: Just note it; verify unboundedness of C_min(p) numerically (if C_min were bounded a finite cover would exist — contradiction with Mordell–Schinzel only for polynomial covers; so unbounded C_min is a separate empirical question!). Compute max C_min(p) for p ≤ 10⁸.

title: Thomas Bloom's unit-fractions Lean library as a base for an 'ES data' formal verification
connection: The Bloom–Mehta Lean project has definitions for unit fraction sums; a formally verified 'ES holds for all n ≤ 10⁶ via these certificates' would be a small but citable deliverable and a test of mathlib infrastructure.
why: Formal verification of computations is now routine; cheap.
first_step: Clone the unit-fractions repo; write a `decide`/`native_decide` based checker for 4/n certificates for n ≤ 10⁴ first.

title: Adaptive C-choice using the factorisation of the previous failure: C_{k+1} = a prime factor of 4C_k p + 1
connection: If q | 4Cp+1 then 4qp·(something)... consider C′ = Cq: 4Cqp + 1 ≡ 1 − q·(4Cp) ... hmm; since 4Cp ≡ −1 mod q, 4Cq'p+1 for C' = C·k ≡ 1 − k mod q. Choosing k ≡ 1 mod q gives q | 4C'p+1 again with a different cofactor — a way to 'reuse' a prime factor q and search the cofactor's residue. This builds chains of C sharing factors: a tree search with algebraic guidance.
why: Algebraically guided chains may hit −1 mod 4C' faster than blind enumeration; and chain structure might be provable (like Euclid's algorithm steps).
first_step: Implement the chain rule and measure chain length to success vs C_min for p ≤ 10⁶.

title: ML: contrastive learning of 'certificate embeddings' to cluster primes by solution structure
connection: Embed each prime by the multiset of its certificate parameters {(c,d)} (as a bag-of-words), cluster, and inspect clusters' arithmetic properties (residues, Legendre profiles). Clusters = 'types of primes' with similar mechanisms.
why: Unsupervised structure discovery; cheap; if clusters align with Legendre profiles it supports the 'Legendre identities' direction.
first_step: Build the feature bags for p ≤ 10⁵; TF-IDF + k-means/UMAP; test cluster–residue alignment via mutual information.

title: ML: train a model to predict f(p) from the factorisations of 4Cp+1, C ≤ 20, to measure how much of f is 'explained' by small C
connection: f(p) is a sum over all (c,d); regressing f(p) on small-parameter data tells what fraction of the count (and of the variance) is small-parameter — if ~90%, the problem is 'nearly local' in parameter space.
why: Dimension-reduction evidence; directs effort to small-parameter theory (class groups of small d) if the fraction is high.
first_step: Compute f(p) and the small-parameter sub-count for p ≤ 10⁶; R² of the regression; plot residuals.

title: Cellular automaton / tag system: encode the greedy-with-backtracking search for 3-term representations as a CA and study its space-time diagram for structure
connection: Rule-based searches sometimes reveal structure via their space-time diagrams (Wolfram's approach); the ES search tree over (x, y) with the two-term test is such a rule system.
why: Recreational/experimental; cheap; near-zero prior of a breakthrough but a possible visual hint.
first_step: Implement and plot for p ≤ 500; stop if nothing visible.
refs: Wolfram, A New Kind of Science

title: Quantum algorithm: Grover search for certificates and complexity of certification
connection: Grover gives √ speedup for unstructured search ↔ ES certificate search space ~ p log p trials, polylog winners.
why: Not a proof route; clarifies computational complexity of finding a certificate (classical best ~ ?).
first_step: Determine the best classical algorithm complexity for finding one ES solution for a given p (repo/verification code) and record whether it's polylog-time heuristically.

title: Shor-type period finding: ES certificate as a hidden-subgroup instance?
connection: HSP over (ℤ/N)^× ↔ ES gate: subgroup generated by divisor classes containing −1.
why: Curiosity mapping; might reveal that certificate-finding reduces to factoring 4Cp+1 (which it does) — so ES search ∈ BQP-easy given factoring.
first_step: Write explicit reduction: ES(p) certificate search ≤ factoring of numbers 4Cp+1 for C ≤ polylog — then note quantum polynomial time.

title: Two-squares in PPA (Zagier windmill) ↔ ES in PPA? A search-problem formulation of windmills
connection: Finding x²+y² = p is in PPA via the Zagier involution (and is known poly-time via Cornacchia) ↔ ES windmill involutions would put ES-search in PPA.
why: If ES-search were PPA-hard or PPA-complete under a natural encoding, that would mean ES's proof must be a parity argument — direct guidance.
first_step: Check the literature on 'Fermat two squares' complexity class membership (e.g. Goldberg–?); attempt to write an ES windmill as a PPA instance (a graph of degree ≤ 2 with p-dependent vertices).

title: Termination analysis tools (ranking functions) applied to an ES search loop
connection: Software verification proves loop termination via ranking functions ↔ ES ⟺ 'for c := 1,2,… test certificate(p,c)' terminates for all p.
why: Automated termination provers (AProVE, Ultimate) fail on number theory, but the framing exposes what invariant is needed: a ranking function = a quantity decreasing until success.
first_step: Write the search loop in C and run a termination analyser to see what it asks for (expect failure; record the missing invariant).

title: Automata: is the set of p (in base b) with a certificate of size ≤ B a regular language? (Büchi/Cobham)
connection: Sets defined by finitely many congruence conditions are b-automatic ↔ finite menus give automatic sets; ES (all primes) is not automatic but the complement of a finite menu is.
why: Cobham's theorem: automatic in two multiplicatively independent bases ⟹ ultimately periodic. Menus are periodic; any 'digital' certificate rule (digit-carry algorithms, B1 hatch) gives automatic sets in one base only — a way to classify digit-based ideas.
first_step: Take a digit-carry ES rule (repo E2 hatch) and compute its automaton; check whether its success set is periodic (then B1) or genuinely base-dependent.

title: Walnut theorem prover for automatic-sequence statements about ES menus
connection: Walnut (Shallit) decides first-order statements about automatic sequences ↔ menu-coverage statements are automatic.
why: Fast way to prove/disprove finite-menu coverings rigorously (although B1 says they fail on primes, Walnut can check for structured n like 4^s + k families).
first_step: Encode the repo's 4^s + k family proofs in Walnut (base 4 automatic) as a test, then try open 4^s + 297 or 15·2^s + 1 families.

title: ECM-style randomised factoring of 4Cp+1 tuned to divisors ≡ −1 mod 4C
connection: ECM finds small factors; ES only needs some divisor in a class ↔ certificate search at astronomical p.
why: Engineering: lets adversarial searches reach p ~ 10^100 cheaply (only smooth parts needed).
first_step: Implement: for C ≤ 10⁴, pull small factors of 4Cp+1 by trial division/ECM and test subproducts for class −1 mod 4C; measure success rate at p ~ 10^100.

title: Automated conjecture generation (Graffiti / TxGraffiti / Ramanujan Machine) on ES statistics
connection: Ramanujan Machine-style search for formulas ↔ conjecture identities for M(p), R(p) moments, minimal certificates.
why: Automated conjecturing may find unexpected exact relations (e.g. between R(p) and class numbers).
first_step: Feed (p, R(p), h(−4p), h(4p), ε_p, n₂(p), Ω(p±1), …) for p ≤ 10⁶ into a Graffiti-like inequality-conjecturer; inspect outputs.

title: Gradient-boosted classifier predicting (★)-line failure from residues: feature importance
connection: ML classifier on p's residues mod m ≤ M predicting low R(p) ↔ which local data matter.
why: Feature importance reveals unexpected moduli or quadratic characters that drive difficulty, possibly a new invariant.
first_step: Train XGBoost on primes ≤ 10⁸ with target log R(p)/log²p, features = p mod m for m ≤ 200 and (q/p) for q ≤ 100; list top features.

title: Neural network certificate generator (learned guessing of (u,C))
connection: Train a model to propose (u,C) for given p, verify exactly ↔ learned certificates.
why: If a small model achieves near-100% top-k accuracy, its learned function may be interpretable (e.g. a rule based on p mod something + a search) — mechanistic interpretability as hypothesis generation.
first_step: Train a transformer on (digits of p) → (u,C) of the smallest certificate for 10⁷ primes; measure top-10 hit rate; probe what it uses.

title: Mechanistic interpretability of a model that 'solves' ES on all tested p
connection: If a network generalises perfectly on out-of-range p, its circuit is an algorithm ↔ a candidate uniform proof idea.
why: Grokking literature shows networks learn modular arithmetic via Fourier features; an ES-solving network would reveal which characters/moduli matter.
first_step: After training (previous item), apply Fourier analysis to embeddings (as in Nanda et al. grokking) to find dominant frequencies.

title: AlphaProof/LLM-prover attempts on ES sub-lemmas (e.g. I3 for structured p families)
connection: AI provers now solve Erdős problems of 'abundance' shape ↔ ES sub-lemmas with explicit families (15·2^s+1, 4^s+297).
why: Open thin families are concrete, bounded-difficulty targets suitable for AI+Lean pipelines.
first_step: Formulate 'ES holds for all 15·2^s + 1' as a Lean statement and give it to an AI prover with repo's window technique as hints.

title: Satisfiability modulo theories with nonlinear integer arithmetic: prove 'ES for n ≡ r mod M' identities automatically
connection: SMT (Z3 NIA) can verify polynomial identities with divisibility ↔ automatic discovery of Mordell-type identities for new classes (non-square).
why: Automated rediscovery of all identity classes mod larger moduli maps exactly which classes have identities (Mordell–Schinzel says square classes never do).
first_step: Use a template x = (a n + b)/c etc. and let a solver search coefficients making 4/n = … an identity on a residue class mod 4·k; enumerate classes covered mod 9240.

title: Hash-based birthday search for collisions between Type I and Type II slices
connection: Birthday paradox: two large lists collide ↔ ES via matching a Type I partial with a Type II partial (meet-in-the-middle).
why: Meet-in-the-middle reformulations sometimes convert existence into collision guarantees (G1 collision column).
first_step: Find a decomposition ES(p) ⟺ L1(p) ∩ L2(p) ≠ ∅ with |L1|,|L2| ≍ √p range; test sizes and collision counts.

title: Cellular automaton encoding of the sieve of certificate classes
connection: 1D cellular automaton marking residues ↔ pictures of the uncovered set.
why: Visual exploration; unlikely to yield theorems but cheap pattern-finding.
first_step: Render a 2D image: row = modulus m = 4uC−1, column = p mod m, highlight −u; overlay hard primes.

title: Compactness argument: ES holds for all n iff a certain closed subset of Ẑ contains no positive integers
connection: The set of n ∈ Ẑ not covered by ET identities is closed ↔ positive integers in it must be handled by non-identity (non-local) certificates.
why: Formalising this would define the 'global part' of ES precisely as integers in a profinite closed set (squares in Ẑ are in it). Then ES ⟺ integer points of that set (non-squares) each have a large certificate.
first_step: Define precisely: K = Ẑ minus ∪(open ET identity classes). Compute K ∩ (ℤ/M) projections for M up to 10⁶; check whether K equals the closure of squares or is larger.

title: Bhavik Mehta / Bloom Lean unit-fractions project as formalisation partner
connection: Bloom–Mehta formally verified the unit-fraction density theorem in Lean (b-mehta.github.io/unit-fractions) ↔ ES sub-results (T1, Mordell reduction, thin families) are formalisable.
why: Existing Lean infrastructure for unit fractions lowers the cost of formalising the repo's elementary results.
first_step: Clone the unit-fractions Lean project; check which definitions (Egyptian sums, rec sums) can be reused for a Lean statement of ES and T1.

title: Fibonacci's Liber Abaci methods for Egyptian fractions as algorithm catalogue
connection: Fibonacci gave several decomposition rules besides greedy ↔ alternative constructive rules for 4/p.
why: Each rule is a candidate certificate family; testing coverage is cheap.
first_step: List Fibonacci's seven rules (via Sigler's translation / Dunton–Grimm summary) and test each as 4/p → 3 terms.

title: Lean: formalise the repo's thin-family proofs ((J)62–(J)80) as computer-checked theorems
connection: Thin families proved computer-assisted ↔ Lean `decide`/`norm_num` certificates.
why: Formal verification gives external-grade confidence and makes them citeable.
first_step: Start with 3·2^s + 1 family: encode window certificate structure in Lean; estimate effort.

title: Formal-conjectures repository: add precise ES-adjacent conjectures (I3_𝒞, F_q lines)
connection: DeepMind's formal-conjectures repo collects Lean statements of open problems ↔ repo's sharp conjectures.
why: Formal statements invite AI provers and disprovers; disprovers could find counterexamples to over-strong conjectures quickly.
first_step: Check if formal-conjectures has ErdosProblems/242; draft Lean statements for I3_𝒞 and F₁₁ as PR candidates (user approval).

title: LLM-assisted literature mining for lemmas of shape 'a fixed integer has a divisor in a residue class'
connection: Semantic search across arXiv for any theorem guaranteeing a divisor of a specific integer in a specified class ↔ ES's core event.
why: Such lemmas are rare and scattered (e.g. in primitive divisor theory, cyclotomy); a targeted mining pass may find a forgotten one.
first_step: Run arXiv full-text search for phrases 'has a divisor congruent to', 'divisor in the residue class', 'prime factor congruent to -1' and screen hits.

title: Benchmark: build an 'ES-hard' dataset for AI provers (statements of sub-lemmas with known answers)
connection: AI-for-math benchmarks ↔ ES sub-lemmas (thin families, slice criteria, T1) with ground truth.
why: Gives the AI community a test bed tied to ES; attracts tool-builders.
first_step: Collect 30 sub-statements (PROVED ones with proofs, CERTIFIED computations, open ones) in a uniform format.

title: Project Euler Egyptian-fraction problems as a source of fast counting algorithms
connection: PE problems on 1/x + 1/y = 1/n and related count solutions fast via divisor enumeration ↔ certificate enumeration engineering.
why: Algorithmic tricks (e.g. enumerating divisors of n² quickly) may speed up censuses.
first_step: Review PE problem forums for unit-fraction problems' best algorithms; benchmark against repo's census code.

title: Decision-tree lower bound: any certificate search querying 'm | p + u' needs ≥ … queries in the worst case
connection: Adversary arguments in query complexity ↔ B1 CRT evasion as an adversary strategy.
why: Formalises B1 as a query-complexity statement: any algorithm with a fixed query order needs unbounded queries (under Dickson); clarifies that the obstacle is order-independent.
first_step: Write the adversary argument formally under Hypothesis H and state the lower bound in terms of menu size.

title: Campos–Griffiths–Morris–Sahasrabudhe 'book algorithm' as a structured search heuristic
connection: The exponential improvement for diagonal Ramsey uses a book-building algorithm controlling red/blue densities; ES certificate search is a two-colour (residue/non-residue) structure problem on divisor sets.
why: The book algorithm is a template for finding large structured objects in a 2-coloured complete structure.
first_step: Colour pairs of prime factors of N by whether their product ratio class is a QR mod e; search for a 'book' configuration implying −1 ∈ Q.
refs: Campos–Griffiths–Morris–Sahasrabudhe, An exponential improvement for diagonal Ramsey, arXiv:2303.09521

title: Condensed/analytic-stack adelic formalism for the integral BM set (honest low-value item)
connection: Clausen–Scholze condensed mathematics gives a uniform framework for topological algebra over all places; the integral Brauer–Manin set of U_n is an adelic topological object.
why: Only a formalism; possibly useful for a clean statement of 'non-BM integral HP failure' families, not for existence.
first_step: Check whether a condensed formulation changes anything in BL's computation; most likely not — record and close.

title: Lean-checked certificate verifier for ES solutions at specific hard primes
connection: A Lean `decide`/`norm_num` proof that 4/p = 1/x+1/y+1/z for explicit p is trivial; a verified checker for large batches (with external computation) mirrors certified-SAT practice.
why: Turns computational evidence (e.g. 10^18 claims) into checkable artefacts — important since the 10^18 claim is an unrefereed preprint.
first_step: Write a Lean function checking ES solutions given (p,x,y,z) and run it on the repo's hard-prime certificates.

title: AlphaProof / LLM provers on campaign lemmas
connection: AI provers (AlphaProof 2024; DeepSeek-Prover, Kimina, Aristotle) solve olympiad-level formal problems; the campaign has many small formal lemmas (sterility, forcing lines, GT1) that are olympiad-like.
why: Automating the verification of small PROVED items frees effort and might find counterexamples to mis-stated lemmas.
first_step: Extract 10 short PROVED lemmas from DISCOVERIES.md into Lean statements and run an available open prover on them.

title: Davies et al. ML-guided intuition: which features predict f(p)?
connection: Davies et al. (Nature 2021) used attribution on trained models to discover knot-invariant and Kazhdan–Lusztig relations; the repo has f_I, f_II for all p ≤ 10^8.
why: A saliency analysis might find an unexpected invariant (beyond p mod small moduli) controlling low-count primes — e.g. a CF or class-number feature.
first_step: Train gradient-boosted trees on features (p mod q for q ≤ 100, n₂(p), class numbers h(−p), h(−4p), CF of √p, Legendre symbols) to predict f(p)/log²p; inspect feature importance.
refs: Davies et al., Advancing mathematics by guiding human intuition with AI, Nature 600 (2021)

title: Hilbert's tenth problem over ℚ (OAI 004, claimed) and Koenigsmann: logical status of ES variants
connection: OAI 004 claims H10 over ℚ is undecidable; Koenigsmann defined ℤ in ℚ by a universal formula. ES is a Π₁ statement once solution sizes are bounded (x ≤ 3n/4, etc.).
why: Being Π₁, ES is 'decided by a counterexample if false'; logic tools say nothing about truth, but undecidability results for families (e.g. 'given polynomial family, does every n have an Egyptian representation') calibrate generality.
first_step: Write ES explicitly as a bounded-quantifier Π₁ sentence and note which generalisations (k/n with arbitrary k, unbounded term count) cross into undecidable territory.
refs: Koenigsmann, Defining ℤ in ℚ, Ann. Math. 183 (2016)

title: Single-fold Diophantine representations (OAI 242, claimed) — uniqueness promise versions of ES
connection: OAI 242 claims every r.e. set has a single-fold Diophantine representation; ES counts solutions (f(n) ≍ polylog), the opposite of single-fold.
why: Records a logic/arithmetic contrast: ES's richness (many solutions) is what makes it plausibly true; single-fold encodings show uniqueness is achievable in general.
first_step: None beyond reading the OAI statement; close unless a uniqueness variant of ES ('exactly one solution of shape X') becomes interesting.

title: Complexity of finding an ES solution: factoring-oracle reduction
connection: Given p, an ES solution is found by factoring a few p-tied integers until a divisor lands in the class; expected polylog many integers. So ES-search is (heuristically) in ZPP^{FACTOR}, and in BQP via Shor.
why: A complexity statement 'ES search is as hard as factoring' (or easier) would be a novel angle; a proof that search is easy for all p would be a constructive ES proof.
first_step: Formalise the reduction and test whether ES certificates can be found without any factoring (e.g. via Coppersmith) for random large p.
refs: Shor, Polynomial-time algorithms for prime factorization…, SIAM J. Comput. 26 (1997)

title: Kolmogorov-complexity view: a least counterexample has a short description
connection: The least ES counterexample (if any) is defined by a short Π₁ formula, so has low description complexity; probabilistic models treat failing p as 'random'.
why: Low-complexity numbers are not random-like; a heuristic tension worth stating (cf. Chaitin) but unlikely to give mathematics.
first_step: Record as a heuristic remark; no computation.
refs: Li–Vitányi, An Introduction to Kolmogorov Complexity (2019)

title: Sarnak Möbius disjointness: is the ES-hardness sequence 'deterministic'?
connection: Sarnak's conjecture: μ is orthogonal to zero-entropy sequences; the indicator of 'ES-hard p' (low normalised count) is a sequence of unknown complexity.
why: Testing correlation of ES-hardness with μ(p−1)-type data or with low-complexity sequences gauges whether hardness has hidden deterministic structure.
first_step: Compute correlations of the hardness indicator with μ((p−1)/4), λ((p+3)/4) and with Sturmian sequences of p.
refs: Sarnak, Three lectures on the Möbius function, randomness and dynamics (2011)

title: SAT/ILP search for a 'prime T1': a non-square class where all certificates of bounded shape fail
connection: A 'prime T1' (structured family of primes with no Type I/II certificates of a bounded shape) is the campaign's sought disproof-shape; SAT/ILP can search residue systems where all bounded-shape certificates fail.
why: Either finds sterile families to a given depth or certifies none exist below a modulus — sharp data for the sterility question.
first_step: Encode depth-K sterility for certificate shapes with C ≤ K as a CRT-consistency SAT instance and search moduli up to 10^6.

title: Arakelov/height view: ES solutions have height ≤ n³-type bound, a Π⁰₁ statement
connection: Positive solutions satisfy x ≤ 3n/4, y ≤ n²-ish and z ≤ n⁴-ish (Curtiss-type bounds), so ES is a Π⁰₁ arithmetic sentence. Heights in Arakelov theory bound points; existence of small-height points is a Siegel-lemma question.
why: Siegel's lemma or geometry of numbers on the torsor might produce small points if a linear structure is present (e.g. Type II at fixed C is linear in some coordinates).
first_step: State precisely the height bounds for positive solutions. Check whether any linear sub-system at fixed (C,d) has a Siegel-lemma solution of the right size.

title: Bounded arithmetic: is the Mordell covering (ES for n ∉ hard classes) provable in IΔ₀ + Ω₁?
connection: Bounded arithmetic proves elementary NT statements whose witnesses are polynomial-time computable. ES for the easy residue classes has explicit polynomial witnesses (Mordell identities), so it is provable in very weak systems.
why: Proof-complexity calibration: a proof of full ES in a weak system would yield a polynomial-time witness algorithm (Buss witnessing). Conversely, if no poly-time deterministic witness algorithm exists, any proof must use strong axioms or non-constructive steps.
first_step: State the witnessing theorem consequence: ES provable in S¹₂ ⇒ a poly-time algorithm outputs (x,y,z) from n. Check whether any deterministic poly-time ES algorithm is known (likely not without factoring).

title: Existential theory of (ℕ, +, |) (Lipshitz/Bel'tyukov) and fixed-C Type II statements
connection: At a fixed level C, 'p has a certificate' is ∃d,k: d | 4Cp+1 ∧ d = 4Ck − 1, an existential formula in (ℕ,+,|) with parameter p. Lipshitz proved the existential theory of (ℤ,+,|) decidable; the ∀p∃ fragment is a different matter.
why: It locates the logical complexity of finite-menu ES statements. A decidable ∀∃ fragment would make 'ES via levels C ≤ C₀' algorithmically decidable, although B1 says such statements are false.
first_step: Check the literature on the decidability of ∀∃ sentences of (ℕ,+,|) (Bel'tyukov, Lipshitz); record whether multiplication becomes definable there.
refs: Lipshitz, The Diophantine problem for addition and divisibility (Trans. AMS 1978)

title: Kolmogorov-complexity view of the sporadic lists (U(n) and Rickards–Stange-type exceptions)
connection: Finite sporadic lists in local-global problems (U(n): six values; RS: 15) have low Kolmogorov complexity only if explained by structure. An algorithmic-information test can flag 'structured' vs 'random' sporadics.
why: Exploratory: a compressible sporadic list suggests a hidden obstruction that might also act at primes.
first_step: Factorisations (computed): 105 = 3·5·7, 2961 = 3²·7·47, 3985 = 5·797, 25305 = 3·5·7·241, 111969 = 3³·11·13·29, 978145 = 5·7·27947. All are ≡ 1 (mod 8); mod 840 they are 105, 441 = 21², 625 = 25², 105, 249, 385, so two lie in square classes mod 840. Next: test whether every sporadic lies in a class mod 840·k that is 'square-like' for U's local model.

title: Machine-learned certificate selectors: features that predict the first working level
connection: Train a classifier on p ↦ least working level (or least u in I3_𝒞), with features such as Legendre symbols of small primes, p mod small moduli and factorisations of p+small. Interpretable models (sparse logistic, decision trees) may expose a structure.
why: This is the data-science native lens. Many repo results (I3_𝒞 u ≤ 39) suggest the selector is simple; a sparse rule could be a conjecture or a lemma candidate.
first_step: Using repo data for p ≤ 10⁹, fit a depth-6 decision tree predicting the least certifying u in I3_𝒞 from (q/p) for q ≤ 50; report accuracy and the tree.

title: The 4-adic structure of words as automata on digits (fixed-letter slices only)
connection: The slot lemma condition depends only on (t,u,v) mod 4 (and p mod 8). Combined with the word equation, the set of valid digit strings (base 2) of (t,u,v) is, for FIXED p, a finite set (so trivially regular). A uniform-in-p carry automaton is impossible because multiplication is not finite-state (Büchi arithmetic cannot define it). What is automatic are fixed-letter slices, e.g. (t,u) fixed and v varying (linear in v; compare tuv − u − v = p).
why: Automata over digits (as in Büchi arithmetic / automatic structures) give a decidable theory of such word sets for fixed p, and 2-adic 'carry' arguments are a native tool (as in Lucas/Kummer theorems).
first_step: Build the base-2 carry automaton for tuv − u − v = p with t,u,v as inputs; compute the language of sign-(−1) words for small p and look for structure across p.

title: Compactness/ultraproduct: a nonstandard ES-failing prime
connection: Tao's Sendov proof takes a sequence of counterexamples with degree → ∞ and analyses a limit object. ES: an ultraproduct of hypothetical failing primes p_k → ∞ is a nonstandard prime p* with no internal certificate; internal theorems (Thm 2.2: M_BM(p*) ≥ c log²p*) hold by Łoś. Seek a contradiction in the nonstandard model (e.g. via a Loeb-measure equidistribution statement).
why: Compactness turns 'all large p' into 'one nonstandard p', making limit-object arguments available.
first_step: Write down which standard theorems about p transfer (counts, character sums) and which 'external' statements (limits of normalised counts) could be proved by Loeb-measure arguments.
refs: arXiv:2012.04125 (Tao, Sendov's conjecture for sufficiently high degree polynomials)

title: SAT search for the smallest profinite obstruction to bounded certificate menus
connection: Konev–Lisitsa used SAT for EDP's C=2. Encode 'no certificate with parameters ≤ K' as residue constraints on p modulo M and use SAT/ILP to find all residue classes mod M consistent with failure; verify that they are exactly squares (B1) and find the minimal K for each M.
why: Cheap automated confirmation of the B1 picture and a generator of hard test cases.
first_step: Encode for M = 840·q (q ≤ 50 prime) and K ≤ 200; compare SAT solutions with the square classes.

title: Certificate-search complexity as a heuristic proxy
connection: Three cubes is 'computation only' because representations are astronomically large. ES certificates are tiny and fast to find; measure the asymptotic cost of the cheapest search (e.g. via Lenstra divisors-in-classes or e-slice scans) as p grows to quantify how 'easy' every p is.
why: If the search cost provably stays polylog for all p in a model, a proof by 'algorithm + analysis' (AKS-style) becomes a natural target.
first_step: Benchmark the cheapest certificate finder on the adversarial primes at 10¹⁸–10²⁵ and fit cost vs log p.

title: Reducibility check automation: verify 'configuration ⇒ certificate' lemmas by computer
connection: The four-colour proof verified each configuration's reducibility by computer. For ES, configuration lemmas of the form 'if p ≡ r (mod M) and 4Cp + 1 has factorisation pattern π then a certificate exists' can be verified symbolically for each (r, π); automate generation and checking of such lemmas.
why: Builds a library of machine-checked partial results that any case-analysis proof would need.
first_step: Implement a checker that, given (M, r, C, pattern), decides via CRT whether a certificate is forced; run over small M and patterns.

title: All-squarefree solutions: fail only at 71, 191, 21 169 among primes ≤ 10⁵
connection: Every prime ≤ 10⁵ except 71, 191, 21169 has an ES solution with x, y, z all squarefree (share 0.15); x squarefree alone never fails (all n ≤ 3000 too).
why: Squarefree denominators are the natural setting for local-global arguments (no prime-power local conditions); a three-exception family is a candidate 'squarefree ES' conjecture. 71 and 191 ≡ 3 (mod 4)!
first_step: Explain 71 and 191 (≡ 7 mod 8, easy for ES but every solution has a square factor); extend census to 10⁷.

title: Proposed 'hall of fame' test set for ES ideas
why: Breadth lanes generate hundreds of candidate connections; a fixed, diverse hard set makes cheap falsification uniform across lanes.
first_step: Add a script that, given a candidate certificate family (as a predicate on (x,y,z) or words), reports which hall-of-fame primes it certifies.

title: Symmetric coordinates
connection: Use s1=x+y+z, s2=xy+xz+yz, s3=xyz and the relation 4s3=ps2 to connect ES to integer-root cubic polynomials.
why: The cubic viewpoint keeps all denominator permutations together and exposes discriminant constraints.
first_step: Search small integer s1,s2 satisfying integral roots of T³−s1T²+s2T−ps2/4.

title: Chinese remainder optimization
connection: Treat parameter selection as a CRT problem with a cost function on the resulting least positive representative.
why: Congruence compatibility and parameter size are distinct, computable parts of certificate design.
first_step: Combine three small valid congruence conditions and optimize the CRT representative by varying their residues.

title: Beatty-sequence denominators
connection: Choose candidate denominators from complementary floor sequences and inspect exact reciprocal residuals.
why: Complementary sequences offer a systematic way to couple rounding errors without claiming an identity.
first_step: For slopes with simple quadratic irrational values, test the first two denominators and factor the residual numerator.

title: Moment inversion for zero counts
connection: Use finite-support moment bounds to estimate the possible mass at zero under measured or proved count moments.
why: This makes the distinction between average abundance and universal positivity explicit without rejecting the approach.
first_step: Solve the small linear program maximizing zero mass subject to the first three empirical moments.

title: Frustration in congruence loops
connection: Identify cycles of local congruence requirements that cannot all be satisfied within a chosen family.
why: Minimal inconsistent loops may indicate which single condition a new family should replace.
first_step: Extract a minimal unsatisfiable set of congruences from a small failed parameter ansatz.

title: Renormalization by eliminating small factors
connection: Integrate out the choices involving the smallest prime factors to obtain an effective residue distribution for the remaining factors.
why: This is exact convolution on a finite group before any approximation is introduced.
first_step: Eliminate prime factors one at a time and track support size, entropy, and target mass.

title: Sparse interpolation of parameter relations
connection: Exploit a small expected monomial support when reconstructing relations among certificate parameters.
why: Sparse reconstruction may discover concise algebraic constraints missed by dense fitting.
first_step: Use a low-degree monomial dictionary on a sample of exact certificates and validate any recovered relation symbolically.

title: Active learning at family boundaries
connection: Choose new examples near the boundary where a simple family selector changes its prediction.
why: Boundary cases may expose missing congruence hypotheses more quickly than uniform sampling.
first_step: Train a shallow selector, query its most ambiguous bounded inputs, and inspect the exact divisibility reasons for each outcome.

title: Out-of-distribution prime tests
connection: Train only on one range or residue stratum and evaluate on genuinely new arithmetic regimes.
why: This detects selectors that memorize local density patterns rather than generalizable mechanisms.
first_step: Hold out an entire congruence class and a larger magnitude range, reporting both separately.

title: Primitive-to-scaled transfer
connection: Track how primitive denominator shapes generate certificates for composite n and which shapes first appear at prime n.
why: This may reveal composition laws without confusing the easy scaling direction with a converse.
first_step: Canonicalize triples by their common gcd and map the resulting primitive shapes to the reduced fraction they represent.

title: Bad reduction of parametrization charts
connection: Identify primes where a symbolic chart or its inverse loses rank or acquires extra components.
why: Those primes may require a different chart and can explain irregular local behavior.
first_step: Compute Jacobian minors and denominator factors for one chart, then list small primes dividing their fixed coefficients.

title: Kronecker's theorem / three-distance theorem for {p/m}
connection: Three-gap theorem for {nα} ↔ distribution of p mod m over m; hits are zeros of a remainder function.
why: Rigid structure of gaps sometimes forces hits; e.g. in ceiling-remainder form, r_p(m) takes values in structured arithmetic progressions on pieces.
first_step: On each piece q, r = qm − p runs through an AP with difference q; the target r | (m+1)/4 — test whether three-distance-type regularity forces hits on long pieces (small q).

title: Flag-algebra / SDP certificates for density inequalities on ES residue menus
connection: Razborov's flag algebras prove density inequalities via SDP; finite residue-menu questions ('what fraction of classes mod M can a menu of shape X cover') are density optimisation problems.
why: SDP duality gives certified upper bounds on coverage — sharpening B1-type statements quantitatively.
first_step: Formulate menu coverage mod M as an LP/SDP and compute the dual bound for small menus.
refs: Razborov, Flag algebras, J. Symbolic Logic 72 (2007)

title: Sum-product incompatibility: subgroup-avoidance across windows vs linear structure of N_e = (p+e)/4
connection: Bourgain–Katz–Tao: no set is nearly closed under both + and × in F_p. ES failure at many windows e forces the prime factors of N_e = (p+e)/4 into structured multiplicative sets mod e (e.g. squares when e is prime ≡ 3 mod 4), while N_e varies linearly in e.
why: If the multiplicative constraints at different e were incompatible with the additive progression N_e, ES would follow; sum-product is the canonical incompatibility principle.
first_step: For e prime ≡ 3 (mod 4), record whether all prime factors of N_e are QRs mod e for the hard primes; check how often this 'square-avoidance' happens across e ≤ 10⁴ compared to random.

title: Chevalley–Warning for the window system modulo e with a forced trivial solution
connection: Chevalley–Warning gives a nontrivial zero when the number of zeros is ≡ 0 (mod char) and a trivial zero exists. For window e (prime), consider the system over F_e in variables (exponent choices) encoding Π q_i^{ε_i} ≡ −1 · (trivial adjustment); design it so ε = 0 is a solution and the degree condition holds, forcing a nonzero ε.
why: The classical algebraic route from 'many variables relative to degree' to existence; here variables = prime factors of N_e.
first_step: Write the system for e = 3, 7, 11 with k prime factors and compute degree vs variables; find k at which Chevalley–Warning applies.

title: Series–parallel networks with k unit resistors realize which rationals? ES as the 3-branch case
connection: The set of resistances of series–parallel networks of k unit resistors is a classical sequence (OEIS). A 3-branch parallel with integer resistors is an ES triple; the general series-parallel set is much larger.
why: Known counts/structure of this set (e.g. via continued fractions) might give a hierarchy argument: n/4 realizable with few resistors ⇒ structure close to ES.
first_step: Look up the OEIS sequence for 'number of distinct resistances with n unit resistors (series–parallel)' and its structural results.

title: Electrical network interpretation
connection: Interpret a denominator or continued-fraction identity as series-parallel resistance reduction.
why: Exact rational network laws may suggest composition operations whose integrality can then be checked.
first_step: Translate short continued fractions into resistor networks and mark operations preserving the required residue classes.

title: Rhythmic subdivisions as identity generators
connection: Translate exact unit-fraction splitting into subdivisions of a common rhythmic cycle, then search for regroupings into three parts.
why: The musical picture is only a representation of rational identities, but may prompt overlooked regroupings.
first_step: Enumerate subdivisions of a 60-slot cycle and retain only regroupings that verify an exact three-unit-fraction equality.

title: Certificate partition functions
connection: Introduce a fugacity for auxiliary size and form a finite partition function whose coefficients count verified certificates.
why: Different fugacities emphasize economical witnesses or high multiplicity without changing the underlying exact count.
first_step: Compute the partition polynomial for a small prime and compare its low-degree coefficients across primes.

title: Quantum-walk-inspired exploration
connection: Compare coherent-walk-inspired search heuristics with classical walks on a finite residue graph, without assuming hardware speedups.
why: Interference patterns may suggest new deterministic orderings of candidate residues.
first_step: Simulate a very small unitary walk and compare the high-amplitude states with shortest target-reaching paths.

title: Adiabatic encodings of bounded ES search
connection: Encode a bounded certificate search as a finite polynomial binary optimization problem and inspect its low-energy states.
why: The encoding itself may expose useful constraints regardless of whether quantum optimization is practical.
first_step: Build an exact tiny QUBO with explicit carry ancillas and verify its ground states by exhaustive enumeration.

title: Transfer-matrix / partition-function view of the ES certificate set
connection: The set of e-slices e ≡ −p (mod 4) with −1 ∈ {ab⁻¹ mod e : ab | N} ↔ a 1-D statistical-mechanics chain whose 'spins' are the prime factors of N and whose Boltzmann weight is the indicator of the product landing in −1 mod e.
why: Positivity of a partition function (Z > 0) is exactly ES(p); stat-mech has tools (Lee–Yang zeros, cluster expansions) for proving positivity/non-vanishing that number theory does not routinely use.
first_step: Write Z_p(β) = Σ_e Σ_{ab|N} exp(−β·dist(ab⁻¹, −1 mod e)) and numerically locate its complex-β zeros for p ≤ 10⁵; check whether zeros avoid the real axis uniformly (Lee–Yang-type) and whether the pattern differs at odd squares.

title: Quantum-chaos / Berry–Tabor view of the e-slice as an integrable billiard
connection: The levels x = (quantity with p in it) of an integrable system have Poisson statistics (Berry–Tabor); the ES certificate x values for fixed p might be modelled by a 2-torus billiard's level set.
why: Poisson statistics would make f(p) ~ Poisson(log²p) with P(f=0) = exp(−c log²p), which is the heuristic ES already relies on; a rigorous Berry–Tabor-type theorem for a suitable flow would be a 'new input'.
first_step: Read Marklof's survey on Berry–Tabor for values of quadratic forms; check whether the e-slice set {(a,b): ab | N, ab⁻¹ ≡ −1 mod e} can be stated as values of a binary form at lattice points.

title: Bethe-ansatz-like counting of ES solutions via a quantum many-body spectrum
connection: Solutions of 4/n = 1/x+1/y+1/z ↔ Bethe roots of a 3-particle system where total 'momentum' 4/n is shared; completeness of Bethe ansatz = existence of a root configuration.
why: Completeness theorems for Bethe ansatz are existence statements proved for every n (e.g. XXX chain for all lengths), by algebraic rigidity — one of the two mechanisms (R) the campaign identified as able to give pointwise results.
first_step: Search 'Bethe ansatz Egyptian fractions' and 'Bethe equations unit fractions'; otherwise try to write the Bethe equations of a 3-magnon sector of a chain of length n and compare with the unit-fraction structure.

title: Casimir / zeta-regularized interpretation of Σ 1/x+1/y+1/z = 4/n
connection: Unit-fraction sums as 'energies' of a vibrating system; zeta-regularized sums 'Σ 1/k' over a finite subset equal 4/n. Totally wild, but 'Casimir energies as Egyptian fractions' might exist in the physics literature.
why: Pure lead-check; cheap.
first_step: Web search 'Casimir energy Egyptian fraction' and 'unit fractions quantum field'; keep only if a nontrivial identity surfaces.

title: Gibbs measure on (C, divisor) pairs and a 'free energy ≥ 0' inequality
connection: Weight each pair (C, d | 4Cp+1, d ≡ −1 mod 4C) by w = C^{−s}; the partition function Z_p(s) for s slightly > 1 converges and ES(p) ⟺ Z_p(s) > 0. Positivity could follow from an identity Z_p(s) = (explicit positive L-value product) + (error) if the error is < main term pointwise.
why: The campaign's M_BM is such a main term; the free-energy framing suggests choosing s to maximise main/error ratio, i.e. a 'temperature' optimisation not previously done.
first_step: Numerically compute Z_p(s) for s ∈ {1.01, 1.1, 1.5, 2} and p ≤ 10⁵; see whether the ratio Z_p(s)/E_C[Z] concentrates better for some s.

title: Chaotic scattering: resonances of 4/n − 1/x − 1/y − 1/z = 0 as a 3-body problem
connection: The equation is the condition for three particles with 'masses' x,y,z to have total 'reduced mass' n/4 — reduced-mass combination 1/μ = Σ 1/m_i. Integer reduced-mass problems may have been posed in recreational physics.
why: Pure lead-check.
first_step: Search 'reduced mass integer unit fractions problem'; drop if nothing.

title: Quantum computing: Shor-like period finding gives a divisor in a residue class?
connection: Shor's algorithm finds the order of a mod N; ES needs a divisor of 4Cp+1 in class −1 mod 4C. Quantum algorithms can find divisors in prescribed classes (by factoring fully), so ES solutions are findable in poly(log p) quantum time *if they exist* — trivially. Non-trivial: is there a quantum 'witness' structure (e.g. a hidden subgroup) that exists for every p?
why: Framing the existence as a hidden-subgroup problem might reveal an algebraic structure (subgroup!) which is what proofs need; low confidence.
first_step: Write the e-slice condition as 'the function g(a,b) = ab⁻¹ mod e on the divisor lattice has −1 in its image' and check whether the image is ever a coset of a subgroup (computation for N ≤ 10⁶).

title: Quantum annealing formulation of ES as QUBO — purely to inspect the energy landscape
connection: Encode the bit-blasted equation as a QUBO; the spectrum of the Ising Hamiltonian (gap between ground state and first excited) across p measures 'hardness'; a gap that scales mildly suggests structure.
why: Cheap curiosity test; may reveal p-dependence of the landscape.
first_step: Build QUBO for p ≤ 200 via standard multiplication gadgets; exact-diagonalise small instances; plot gap vs p.

title: Physics redux: the C-form as a 1-D 'Ising chain in a field' where the field is the character χ and the spins are prime factors — exact solvability (transfer matrix) of the per-C partition function
connection: #{a | N: a ≡ −1 (4C)} = (1/φ) Σ_χ χ(−1) Π_{q^e ∥ N} (1 + χ(q) + … + χ(q)^e) is literally a sum over 'external fields' χ of a product of single-site partition functions — an exactly solvable (non-interacting) model. ES failure = destructive interference across χ. The physics intuition: non-interacting spins in φ(4C) different fields; the total vanishes iff … This is exactly the structure where 'Lee–Yang' and 'sign problem' intuitions apply: the sum over χ is a sum with signs (χ(−1) = ±1 and complex χ(q)).
why: Just the exact formula in physics clothing; but the 'sign problem' analogy suggests looking at |Σ| vs Σ|·| — the ratio measures cancellation; and the structure 'product of single-site terms' means the count is a *Fourier transform of a product* — a convolution on the group, which is where Kneser/subset-sum structure enters (item on additive combinatorics).
first_step: Compute the cancellation ratio (count)/(Σ_χ |Π|)/φ for failing vs winning (p, C); see whether failures are 'maximal cancellation' events with a recognisable pattern.

title: R(p) as a partition function: Z(β) = Σ over trial pairs of exp(−β·cost) and the β→∞ limit
connection: Statistical mechanics: count of certificates = zero-temperature limit of a partition function over the trial set 𝓡 with energy = 'distance from divisibility' ↔ R(p).
why: Smooth relaxations (finite β) are analytically tractable (sums of exponentials of residues) and could be bounded below; the question is whether a β-interpolation lower bound survives β → ∞.
first_step: Define E(u,C) = ((p+u) mod (4uC−1))/(4uC−1) and compute Z(β) = Σ e^{−βE} for p ≤ 10⁵; check monotone behaviour of log Z(β) vs log R(p) at large β.

title: Spectral form factor / pair correlation of 'certificate moduli' 4uC−1 dividing p+u
connection: Quantum chaos tools on number-theoretic sequences ↔ distribution of the set of successful (u,C) per p.
why: Clustering/repulsion of certificates would indicate dependencies affecting zero probability.
first_step: For each p compute the set of successful (u,C); measure nearest-neighbour spacing distribution in log-scale over p ≤ 10⁶.

title: Ising-like spin model: the BM character as a spin and T(p) as magnetisation
connection: T(p) = Σ (−uB/p)/φ(4uB) is a weighted sum of ±1 spins over pairs ↔ magnetisation of a spin system with couplings from multiplicativity.
why: Spin-glass bounds or correlation inequalities (Griffiths/GKS) give pointwise inequalities for ferromagnetic systems; multiplicativity (−uB/p) = (−u/p)(B/p) is a product spin structure (Mattis model).
first_step: Write T(p) = Σ_{u,B} s_u s'_B w(u,B) with s_u = (u/p): it's a Mattis-type bilinear form; compute the max over arbitrary sign patterns vs actual to see how far from worst case.

title: Annealed vs quenched averages for certificate counts
connection: Disordered systems: quenched average E[log Z] vs annealed log E[Z] ↔ log R(p) average vs log of average.
why: A large gap indicates rare-event dominance (some p with huge counts, e.g. via Linnik), which affects lower-tail heuristics.
first_step: Compute E[log(1+R(p))] vs log E[R(p)] over primes in dyadic ranges up to 10⁸.

title: Music: Egyptian fractions as rhythms (tuplets) and polyrhythm decompositions
connection: Splitting a measure of length 4/p into three unit-length subdivisions ↔ polyrhythmic tuplets in music notation.
why: Outreach and pattern-hearing; sonification of certificate counts over p could reveal periodicities the eye misses.
first_step: Sonify R(p) over primes ≤ 10⁵ (pitch = R/M) and listen for regular structure; or render tuplet patterns.

title: Music: just intonation ratios and 4/p as an interval split into three superparticular-like steps
connection: Superparticular ratios (n+1)/n compose intervals; Egyptian fractions relate via 1/n differences ↔ decomposing intervals.
why: Loose analogy; possible cute reformulation for outreach only.
first_step: Check whether 1 + 4/p = Π(1 + 1/x_i)-type decompositions (multiplicative Egyptian) relate to ES (they don't directly; record the multiplicative variant as a separate question).

title: 2D quantum harmonic oscillator: (★) ⟺ in an oscillator with frequencies (u,B), level p is the highest level with degeneracy 4C − 1
connection: Energy levels n = au + bB of a 2D oscillator with commensurate frequencies have degeneracy N(n; u,B) ↔ ES words p = g_t(u,B) are 'last levels before the degeneracy reaches t' (with particle–hole-type symmetry N(n) + N(g_t − n) = t).
why: Exact physics dictionary; degeneracy-counting via semiclassical (Weyl) asymptotics plus exact Ehrhart corrections is a mature toolkit. Mostly a reframing, but the 'degeneracy jump' language may suggest spectral (trace-formula) approaches to counting all (u,B) at once.
first_step: Write Z(β) = Σ_n N(n;u,B) e^{−βn} = 1/((1 − e^{−βu})(1 − e^{−βB})) and express 'p is a jump level' via residues of Z at roots of unity (Sylvester waves); sum over (u,B) formally.

title: Effective resistance A/p of a 3-node ladder network
connection: In the fan network with unit conductances, the effective resistance between a and the sink is (M⁻¹)₁₁ = A/p. So ES₅(p) ⇔ a three-node ladder network with integer conductances to ground and total 'tree count' p has R_eff(a,s) = A/p with A a non-residue mod p.
why: Electrical-network theory has exact theorems on which rationals are resistances of networks with k unit resistors (series–parallel ↔ continued fractions). The ES sign becomes a residuosity property of a physical quantity.
first_step: Enumerate rational resistances of networks with ≤ 12 unit resistors (OEIS A048211 family); check whether non-residue numerators A/p appear at small resistor counts for every p ≡ 1 (4) < 2000.

title: Ising model on F_p: ES₅ failure = zero-energy configuration of a frustrated ferromagnet
connection: Put spins σ_v = (v/p) on F_p. ES₅ failure (no bichromatic edge) means the Legendre configuration is a ground state of the ferromagnetic Ising Hamiltonian on F_p. Statistical mechanics has Peierls/contour arguments for when ground states must have domain walls.
why: A Peierls-type argument combines an 'external field' (Legendre symbol bias on short intervals) with graph connectivity. It is a native tool not obviously tried.
first_step: Compute, per component of F_p, the fraction of +spins; check how large monochromatic components get (ES₅ only needs one bichromatic edge somewhere, so monochromatic components are compatible with ES₅).

title: Farey-fraction spin chain (Kleban–Özlük) partition function and the ES words
connection: Kleban–Özlük's Farey spin chain has a partition function built from products of matrices [[1,0],[1,1]] and [[1,1],[0,1]], and its states are Farey fractions. ES words correspond to specific length-3 HJ blocks, so a restricted partition function counts them.
why: Statistical mechanics of number-theoretic chains has exact phase-transition results; a 'Legendre-field' coupling would make the ES sign a magnetization.
first_step: Define Z_p(β, h) = Σ_{A} e^{−β·r(p/A)} (A/p)^{h}; compute for p < 10⁴ and look at the h-derivative at β → ∞ (the min-length sign).
refs: Kleban–Özlük, A Farey fraction spin chain (CMP 1999)

title: Knauf's number-theoretic spin chain and Riemann ζ: a ζ-like Dirichlet series for HJ lengths
connection: Knauf's spin chain partition function is ζ(s−1)/ζ(s). An analogous chain with HJ (by-excess) matrices and a quadratic-character field might have a Dirichlet-series partition function whose coefficients encode λ(p).
why: If the partition function is an L-function quotient, analytic properties (zeros/poles) would control its coefficients.
first_step: Compute Σ_{p,A} p^{−s} x^{r(p/A)} (A/p) numerically and try to identify it as an L-function combination.
refs: Knauf, On a ferromagnetic spin chain (CMP 1993)

title: Statistical-mechanics partition function over all ES solutions and Lee–Yang zeros
connection: Define Z_n(β) = Σ_{solutions} (xyz)^{−β}. ES(n) ⇔ Z_n ≢ 0. Lee–Yang-type theorems locate zeros of partition functions with ferromagnetic structure. A family Z(n, β) analytic in n-related variables might have provably non-vanishing coefficients.
why: Speculative, but it is the stat-mech native form of 'nonempty'; the Dirichlet series Σ_n Z_n(β) n^{−s} is a height zeta function of the threefold 𝒰.
first_step: Compute the height zeta function Σ_n Σ_{sol} n^{−s}(xyz)^{−β} numerically; check for Euler-product structure.

title: Fractional quantum Hall hierarchy: the chain matrix as a K-matrix and the ES sign as an anyon-theory class
connection: Haldane–Halperin hierarchy states have tridiagonal K-matrices whose filling is an HJ continued fraction. The anyon theory is the discriminant form of K on ℤ^r/Kℤ^r (here ℤ/p). ES₅(p) ⇔ a 3-level hierarchy state with det K = p whose ℤ/p anyon braiding form is in the non-square class.
why: Abelian Chern–Simons theory classifies anyon theories with ℤ/p fusion into two classes (by the Gauss sum and chiral central charge). Physics constraints such as Gauss–Milgram relate the class to the signature and to spin structure.
first_step: Write the topological spins θ_x = e^{πi x²A/p} for the fan K-matrix; compute the Gauss–Milgram sum (odd/fermionic version) and relate it to the slot lemma.
refs: Wen, Quantum Field Theory of Many-Body Systems ch. 7 (K-matrix)

title: Resistor-network rung: n/4 as the resistance of any 3-resistor integer network
connection: Three integer resistors in parallel give ES. The other 3-resistor topologies (series + parallel mixes: x + (y‖z), (x + y)‖z) give other Diophantine conditions. 'Every n/4 is realised by some 3-resistor network' is a rung that contains ES.
why: Calibration: it shows whether ES's difficulty is specific to the all-parallel topology. A cheap computation decides it for small n.
first_step: For n < 10⁶, check realisability of n/4 by each 3-resistor topology; list the n realisable only via the parallel one and those not realisable at all.

title: Physics: renormalisation-group picture of the HJ ladder λ(p) ≤ L as depth of a hierarchical lattice
connection: Hierarchical (Berker/Migdal–Kadanoff) lattices are built by iterated substitution. Chain matrices of length L are hierarchical networks of depth L. 'Some depth-3 hierarchical network with τ = p has a non-square pairing' is ES₅. RG flow of the resistance under substitution is a Möbius (continued-fraction) map.
why: The RG viewpoint makes HJ length a 'number of RG steps', and statistical physics has fixed-point and universality tools for such flows (though arithmetic exactness is needed here).
first_step: Write the resistance RG map for the ladder and identify the HJ digits as couplings; check whether the sign is an RG invariant mod 2.

title: Probability: 1/x + 1/y + 1/z as the rate of the minimum of three exponentials
connection: If T_i ~ Exp(mean x_i) are independent, min T_i has mean 1/Σ(1/x_i). ES ⇔ the minimum of three exponential clocks with integer means has mean n/4. Equivalent for discrete clocks: the first success among three periodic processes.
why: Reformulation only; might suggest probabilistic couplings to count solutions.
first_step: Low priority; note.

title: Beurling generalized integers: build a system where some generalized prime fails ES
connection: ES's Type II needs divisors of the additive shift 4Cp + 1; Beurling systems keep multiplicative structure but destroy additive structure. In a Beurling system with integers 'close to' ℕ (Diamond–Montgomery–Vorhauer type), ES may fail infinitely often.
why: A Beurling counterexample would prove that any ES proof must use additive structure beyond the multiplicative/PNT statistics — a 'barrier theorem'.
first_step: Define ES for Beurling integers N_P (with an addition borrowed from R), construct a random Beurling system and test ES for its primes numerically.

title: Probabilistic 'Schinzel world': random rationals a/b with b prime — what fraction are 3-term sums?
connection: Luca–Pappalardi/Mond–Portier give x(log x)³ ≪ Σ_{p≤x} A₃(p) ≪ x(log x)³(log log x)², i.e. A₃(p) is about (log p)⁴ on average over primes (up to loglog); heuristically a random numerator a ≤ p is representable with probability ≈ (log p)⁴/p (an average-based heuristic, not a theorem about individual p). ES says a = 4 always is: 4 is special because small numerators have more representations.
why: Makes precise that ES is about the small-numerator end of a distribution whose bulk is sparse; methods that see only averages over a cannot reach a = 4.
first_step: Compute #representations of a/p as a function of a for fixed p ~ 10^4; fit decay in a.

title: ES on average over number fields: for random real quadratic K, how often does rational ES need units?
connection: For many K, rational ES solutions over O_K may be integer solutions (no units needed). Statistics of 'units needed' across K measure how often integer ES is the bottleneck.
why: If, for a positive proportion of K, all p have non-unit solutions of a new type (genuinely quadratic denominators without units), these give a new integer-adjacent mechanism.
first_step: For D ≤ 100 and p ≤ 1000 count solutions with non-rational denominators not using units (bounded height).

title: Random thinning: keep each integer as a denominator independently with probability ρ — threshold ρ_c(p)
connection: With #ES(p) ≈ c log²p solutions, a random ρ-thinning keeps each solution with probability ρ³; the expected surviving count is c ρ³ log²p, so failures appear when ρ ≲ (log p)^{−2/3}.
why: A purely probabilistic world with an explicit threshold; comparing with the observed failure rates of structured thinnings (norms, Beatty) shows which thinnings are 'random-like'.
first_step: Simulate ρ ∈ {0.5, 0.3, 0.2} on all solutions for p < 2·10^4 and compare failure fractions with the Poisson prediction exp(−ρ³ #ES(p)).

title: Transfer: Selberg–Delange / Landau for counting H-confined N_C
connection: Counts of integers composed of primes in a set of Dirichlet density δ follow Landau–Selberg–Delange ~ c x (log x)^{δ−1}.
why: Gives the precise heuristic per-C failure probability, the input of ES Poisson models.
first_step: Compute δ_C = |H_C|/φ(4C) maximal over subgroups H_C ∌ −1 (which is 1/2 when −1 ∉ index-2 subgroups) and derive the model.

title: Meta: Poisson model predicts largest exception for each m — test at m = 4 by 'virtual exceptions'
connection: Under the PW Poisson model P(fail) ≈ exp(−(log p)³/m · κ), compute the expected number of exceptions beyond 10^18 for m = 4: if astronomically small, ES's verification is 'model-complete'.
why: Clarifies what verification to 10^18 means under the best available model.
first_step: Fit κ from m = 8..15 exception data, compute Σ_{p > 10^18} P(fail) for m = 4.

title: Result: CRT avoidance density of ES certificate families decays like exp(−c (ln X)³), c ≈ 0.028
connection: Fraction δ(X) of residues in Mordell's hard classes (prime-like) that avoid every Type I family (p ≡ −f mod 4ad, f | 4a²d+1) and Type II family (p ≡ −e mod 4ab, e | a+b) with ad, ab ≤ X: δ(100) = 7.8e-2, δ(1000) = 1.2e-4, δ(1778) = 9e-6; ln δ/(ln X)³ ≈ 0.025–0.030 stable over X = 56..1778 (2·10⁶ samples).
why: This is exactly the Poisson/independence prediction (expected number of hitting families ~ (log X)³, matching Pomerance–Weingartner's (log p)³/m scaling): ES's certificate families behave like independent events at the level of residues. EVIDENCE only; Chebotarev makes δ(X) the exact density of primes unsolved by families ≤ X.
first_step: Extend to X = 10⁴ with 10⁸ samples (vectorised, memory-bounded) to test whether the exponent 3 persists or creeps.

title: Connection: correlation between families measured by survivor statistics
connection: In the residue model, families are independent if δ(X) equals ∏(1 − density of family). Comparing the observed δ(X) with the independent product quantifies correlation exactly (no primes needed).
why: Correlation is the one unknown dividing-line coordinate for ES; this is a direct, cheap measurement.
first_step: Compute ∏_{families ≤ X}(1 − |res|/φ(m)·…) (careful with non-unit residues) vs observed δ(X).

title: Connection: the m/p family in the residue model
connection: Run the same CRT-avoidance computation for m = 5..15 (Type I: f | m a² d + 1, m a d | p + f; Type II: e | a+b, m a b | p + e) and compare δ_m(X) with PW's exception tables.
why: If δ_m(X) predicts the observed largest exceptions for m = 8..15 (e.g. 241 for m = 8), the residue model is validated on cases with actual failures — the strongest available heuristic check for m = 4.
first_step: Parametrise scripts/z52b_dividing_avoid.py by m; note PW's exceptions are for all n, not just primes.

title: nx(n): number of distinct first denominators
connection: nx(n) = #{x : some solution has this smallest denominator}: 1,2,2,1,3,3,4,3,4,3,6,2,… (not in OEIS); at primes correlates like U (ρ=−0.65 with L(1,χ_p)).
why: nx is the 'first-step branching' of the greedy tree; lower bounds on nx(p) are ES; it is the quantity a sieve over x controls.
first_step: Fit nx(p) vs log p (likely ≍ log p, not log²p) and check whether nx(p) ≥ 1 has a shorter proof form (one-shift divisibility).

title: Is U(p)/log²p approximately lognormal?
connection: Histogram the residual; tails determine the probability of U(p)=0 under a smooth model — heavy lower tail would make finitely-many-exceptions heuristics fragile.
why: LOWER_TAIL_* memos study the lower tail of (★); the same for U is cheap here.
first_step: Fit normal/skew-normal to the residual and compute the predicted P(U(p) ≤ 5) vs observed (only p ≤ 17).

title: Composite U(pq) depends weakly on U(p), U(q): log U(pq) ≈ 3.0 + 0.20 log U(p) + 0.11 log U(q) + 0.26 log n
connection: Over 5 668 odd semiprimes pq ≤ 30 000 (p < q), counts at pq are mostly governed by size, mildly by the factors' counts.
why: ES at composites reduces to primes for existence, but counts are 'more than inherited' — composite n have many non-inherited solutions; irrelevant to ES existence but relevant to count heuristics on all n.
first_step: Separate inherited (scaled from 4/p or 4/q) and non-inherited solutions at pq.

title: Bounded U-certificate size: Vmin(p) ≤ 116 for all primes p ≡ 1 (4) ≤ 3·10⁶
connection: Least v ∈ 4ℤ ∪ (8ℤ−p), v ≥ 3, with p+v having a divisor ≡ −1 (mod v): records 3 (5), 4 (17), 7 (97), 8 (457), 23 (1009), 87 (2521), 116 (3361) and no further record up to 3·10⁶; 99.9% quantile 31, mean 4.0.
why: A bounded-v version of U ('U_V: some v ≤ V works') is a finite union of single-shift divisor problems; if true for V = 116 it reduces ES at primes to finitely many 'p + v has a divisor ≡ −1 (mod v)' events — exactly the shape where single-shift laws (EXSET_SHIFT_DIVISORS Thm 2.2) apply, though the joint failure probability must still be bounded.
first_step: Extend the Vmin census to 10⁹ at primes; check whether records resume (each single-shift failure has probability ≍ (log p)^{−1/2}, so a fixed finite V must eventually fail infinitely often under independence — the data test that heuristic).

title: Lower envelope of U(p): extreme-value fit
connection: The minimum of U(p)/log³p over windows of N primes should behave like an extreme value of the (approximately lognormal) residual — Gumbel scaling predicts min ≈ median·exp(−σ√(2 log N)).
why: If minima fall faster than Gumbel, there are arithmetic 'hard families' (e.g. lcm+1) beyond the bulk; slower ⇒ bulk-dominated. Distinguishes the two pictures of ES hardness.
first_step: Estimate σ of residual log U at 10⁶/10⁷ (≈ 0.25?) and compare predicted vs observed window minima and the 2·10⁵ global minimum (2521).

title: Decay of parameter correlations
connection: Measure how correlation between successes at C and D depends on gcd(C,D), distance, and shared small factors.
why: Arithmetic dependence may have a usable organization even without independence.
first_step: Estimate pairwise success correlations for C,D≤40 after grouping pairs by gcd.

title: Entropy of divisor residues
connection: Measure how rapidly the residue distribution spreads as prime-power factors are added to a divisor set.
why: Entropy gives a quantitative description of concentration in a proper subgroup or coset.
first_step: Convolve the two-choice residue measures factor by factor for small factored auxiliary integers.

title: Rare prime strata as separate models
connection: Partition primes by combinations of small character values and build separate count models for sparse strata.
why: Mixture distributions can hide strong structure in an exceptional tail.
first_step: Choose three small character labels and compare the full count histogram within each nonempty stratum.

title: Complement-residue bias correction
connection: Compare a naive uniform divisor-residue heuristic with the exact complementary-divisor pairing constraints.
why: Correcting this built-in dependence may sharpen predictions of rare zero counts.
first_step: Derive the paired-residue count identities for small moduli and fit a constrained null model.

title: VC dimension of certificate families
connection: View each parametrized identity as a subset of sampled primes and estimate the combinatorial complexity of that set system.
why: Low complexity might explain why small representative samples reveal much of the coverage structure.
first_step: Search for shattered subsets of size up to five in a bounded incidence matrix.

title: Spin systems for factor selection
connection: Assign a binary spin to each available prime factor and make the total residue the observable of the selected product.
why: This is an exact finite statistical-mechanics model of divisor selection when multiplicities are tracked.
first_step: For a squarefree auxiliary integer, compute the residue distribution by both spin enumeration and divisor enumeration.

title: Zeros of counting polynomials
connection: Study complex zeros of finite certificate-generating polynomials as descriptors of changes in count structure.
why: Root geometry can distinguish count distributions, but no phase-transition or positivity theorem is assumed.
first_step: Compute roots of low-degree count polynomials and check whether unusual root patterns correlate with sparse witness sets.

title: Replica overlap diagnostics
connection: Take two independently sampled certificates for the same p and measure how many factor choices or denominator components they share.
why: Overlap distributions distinguish a broad witness space from many variants of one mechanism.
first_step: Sample bounded certificates uniformly after deduplication and histogram their factor-overlap sizes.

title: Finite-size scaling as a falsifiable heuristic
connection: Compare rescaled distributions of least witness cost across increasing prime ranges.
why: A scaling collapse could propose a growth law; failure of collapse is also informative.
first_step: Fit the scaling on one prime range and test it on a larger disjoint range with identical search rules.

title: Density of states near valid certificates
connection: Count parameter assignments by exact residual size and divisibility defect rather than only success or failure.
why: Near-zero abundance might suggest a correction lemma or reveal that approximate solutions are misleading.
first_step: Compute the joint histogram of residual numerator and gcd defect for a small parameter box.

title: Random-matrix baselines for family incidence
connection: Compare singular values of the actual family-prime incidence matrix with matrices preserving its row and column sums.
why: This can detect collective arithmetic structure beyond individual family success rates.
first_step: Generate degree-preserving shuffled matrices and compare their leading singular values with the original.

title: Polynomial identity testing with deterministic closure
connection: Use randomized evaluations to reject false formulas quickly, then perform exact symbolic verification on survivors.
why: Random testing is a filter, never the final proof of an identity.
first_step: Generate a batch of candidate identities, filter at random integer points, and expand only the survivors.

title: Smooth-order factorization steering
connection: Choose auxiliary parameters whose likely useful factors have smooth multiplicative-group order, then test a p−1-style factoring strategy.
why: This is a construction-and-search heuristic, not a claim that such factors always exist.
first_step: For C≤100, compare certificate usefulness of factors found cheaply by a small smooth-order budget.

title: Las Vegas certificate discovery
connection: Allow random candidate generation but accept outputs only after deterministic exact verification.
why: Randomness then affects runtime rather than the correctness of reported witnesses.
first_step: Design a randomized parameter sampler with explicit timeouts and an independent certificate checker.

title: Small-bias parameter schedules
connection: Replace unrestricted random residues with a small explicitly generated sample space and measure which character tests it fools.
why: A derandomized schedule may preserve relevant coverage statistics if the test class is identified.
first_step: Construct a tiny small-bias distribution for a selected finite group and compare its character averages with those of uniform sampling.

title: Property-based arithmetic testing
connection: Generate structured random inputs satisfying a family's hypotheses rather than arbitrary integers.
why: This efficiently catches transcription errors while remaining only a development check.
first_step: Design generators for divisibility-compatible parameters and test the cleared identity and positivity separately.

title: Random matrix statistics of the ES solution-count sequence f(p)
connection: f(p) (number of 4/p solutions) ↔ eigenvalue-count statistics; ask whether the normalized fluctuations of f(p)/log²p follow a known RMT law (GUE/GOE/Poisson) or a Selberg-class law.
why: If f(p) behaves like a 'spectral count' of some operator, then a lower bound f(p) ≥ 1 could be a spectral gap statement instead of a sieve statement.
first_step: Compute f(p) for primes up to 10⁷ (repo has data), fit the distribution of f(p)/E[f] and its two-point correlation along primes; compare to Poisson and to divisor-function moments (Deshouillers–Dress–Tenenbaum arcsine law).

title: Percolation threshold on the 'divisor-in-class' bipartite graph across C
connection: Build the bipartite graph with left vertices C ∈ [1,X], right vertices residue classes mod 4C, edge if 4Cp+1 has a divisor ≡ −1 mod 4C. ES(p) is 'some left vertex has its target edge'. Percolation thresholds as X grows ↔ how fast the first winning C appears.
why: The first winning C, C_min(p), is a natural 'order parameter'; its growth law (log p? p^ε?) is what any pointwise proof must beat.
first_step: Compute C_min(p) for all primes p ≤ 10⁷ (cheap), fit distribution; check whether the repo already has this (git grep 'C_min' or 'smallest C').

title: Entropy of the ES solution set as a function of p: 'thermodynamic limit' test
connection: Define S(p) = log f(p). Is S(p) ≈ 2 log log p + c with bounded fluctuations (like an extensive quantity) or heavy-tailed? Thermodynamic self-averaging would give concentration; concentration is the enemy of counterexamples.
why: If S(p) concentrates with sub-Gaussian tails around 2 log log p, counterexamples are 'large deviations' and a large-deviation principle could be a route to an unconditional bound at least for 'typical' primes in explicit sets.
first_step: Use the repo's f(p) data (p ≤ 10⁸) to fit the tails of S(p) − mean; compare with Erdős–Kac-type normal law for ω(4Cp+1).

title: Turbulence-style intermittency statistics for f(p)
connection: Multifractal/intermittent behaviour of f(p) across p (moments ⟨f^q⟩ scaling anomalously) would indicate heavy tails; the campaign only has means and almost-all results.
why: Moment scaling exponents distinguish 'log-normal' from 'Poisson' models of f(p); the lower tail (f = 0) is the whole question.
first_step: Compute ⟨f(p)^q⟩ for q = −2..4 over primes in dyadic ranges up to 10⁸ using repo data; fit scaling exponents.

title: Entanglement-entropy-style 'area law' for solution counts across Type I/Type II
connection: f_I(p) and f_II(p) are counted separately; their mutual information (over p) measures how independent the two mechanisms are. If nearly independent, P(f=0) ≈ P(f_I=0)·P(f_II=0), squaring the exponent in the heuristic.
why: A quantitative independence statement (even EVIDENCE) sharpens the target: proving only f_I ≥ 1 or only f_II ≥ 1 may be the better-defined problem.
first_step: From repo data, compute correlation of f_I(p), f_II(p) and of their indicator-of-zero across p ≤ 10⁸; compare conditional distributions.

title: Hash-function / pseudorandomness: treat (p ↦ prime factorisation of 4Cp+1) as a PRG and ES as 'PRG never outputs the all-miss pattern'
connection: Cryptographic pseudorandomness would *predict* P(miss) ≈ exp(−c log²p) and that misses happen for some p; ES asserts that they never happen — i.e. the map is detectably non-pseudorandom in the lower tail.
why: Forces a clear statement: either ES's 'never' is a coincidence of the small-count regime (and there IS a counterexample), or there is a structural correlation across C. The question 'which' is the campaign's central dilemma; the crypto framing suggests testing *higher-order correlations* across C.
first_step: Measure pairwise and triple correlations between the events 'C wins' and 'C′ wins' for p ≤ 10⁷; compare to independent model.

title: Carmichael's λ and the group structure of (ℤ/4C)^× : choosing C with (ℤ/4C)^× cyclic of small order to make −1 'easy to hit'
connection: For C = 1: (ℤ/4)^× = {±1}; a single factor ≡ 3 mod 4 suffices. For C = p': (ℤ/4p')^× ≅ ℤ/2 × ℤ/(p'−1). −1 is the unique element of order 2 in the cyclic part… the chance a random subset product hits −1 is ≈ 1/φ(4C) per product, but the number of products is 2^ω. Choosing C with φ(4C) small relative to 2^{ω(4Cp+1)}: C prime-power-ish and 4Cp+1 very composite.
why: Optimising the choice of C-family by group structure is a cheap heuristic refinement; could yield a family of C where the win probability is bounded below (e.g. C with 4C | something).
first_step: For p ≤ 10⁶, among winning C ≤ 10⁴, histogram φ(4C)/2^{ω(4Cp+1)}.

title: Probability: ES failure as the event that a 'random' prime avoids infinitely many independent residue classes — a Borel–Cantelli on the covering classes
connection: If p's residues mod a (for a ≡ −1 mod 4C) were independent uniform, P(p avoids class r_{C,a} for all (C,a) ≤ K) = Π (1 − 1/a) ≈ exp(−Σ 1/a) → 0 as K → ∞ since Σ_{a ≡ −1 (4C)} 1/a diverges (like (1/φ(4C)) log). Borel–Cantelli direction 'infinitely many events occur a.s.' — the point is that for ONE p the events are deterministic, but the independence heuristic says failure is impossible; a rigorous version is the Kubilius model / Turán–Kubilius for 'residues of p across moduli'.
why: The Kubilius model gives rigorous approximation of arithmetic functions by independent random variables *on average over p*; its pointwise version is the Erdős–Kac-type concentration. Here we need 'for each p' — but a Turán–Kubilius variance bound over p ∈ [X, 2X] gives that the number of p ≤ X avoiding all classes ≤ K is ≪ X·exp(−c log K) + error; with K ≈ X^ε this is the Vaughan-type exceptional set bound by elementary means. Re-derive and compare constants.
